items.abstract: <jats:p>Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.</jats:p>
title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity

items.abstract: <jats:p>Computer network security is a critical concern in the era of increasing cyber threats. Traditional intrusion detection systems rely on handcrafted rules and statistical features that fail to capture the complex topological relationships inherent in network traffic. This paper proposes a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for computer network anomaly detection that models network traffic as dynamic graphs and applies Graph Attention Networks (GAT) combined with Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) for spatial-temporal anomaly detection. We further provide a comprehensive algorithm efficiency evaluation covering inference time, memory usage, throughput, and floating-point operations. Experiments on the CIC-IDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 datasets demonstrate that the proposed GAT-GRU model achieves 95.23% F1-score and 0.98 AUC, outperforming baseline methods including MLP, GCN, and GraphSAGE, while maintaining acceptable computational overhead for real-time deployment.</jats:p>
title: Graph neural network-based computer network anomaly detection and algorithm efficiency evaluation
